name: Action Policies and Approval Thresholds
question: Is the agent allowed to take this action, right now?
summary: Controls on what the agent does, not only what it says. Each tool is rated by impact, and every call is checked against a written policy when it runs: deny by default, scoped and short-lived credentials, limits on amounts and recipients, and an approval threshold above which a person must say yes. This is sometimes called zero-trust runtime governance.
useCases: Agents with tools that write: payments, emails, database changes, deployments
Multi-agent systems where one agent’s output drives another’s actions
Anywhere a successful prompt injection must not turn into a real action

items.detail: allow or deny at runtime, written as code
a gate on high-impact or irreversible actions
isolated execution for code, files and network
every call, argument and decision logged
caps on spend, calls and time; instant stop

steps: List every tool and rate its impact: read, write or irreversible
Give each task the narrowest credentials it needs and make them expire
Put a policy engine between the agent and its tools, denying by default
Set approval thresholds for high-impact actions (the pause itself is covered in Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints) and alert on anomalies in the audit log
pitfalls: Too many approval prompts train people to click Approve without reading
One broad API key shared across agents defeats least privilege
Policies drift from reality unless they are versioned and tested like code
remember: Deny by default, scope every call, set the approval line in code.
caption: Every tool call meets the policy gate. Reads run, risky writes wait for a person, and destructive calls are denied.

code.text: def run_tool(task, tool: str, args: dict):

steps.title: Rate every tool’s impact
steps.text: Reads, writes and irreversible actions get different treatment. A tool that isn’t listed is “unknown” and will be denied.

steps.title: Issue a narrow, short-lived credential
steps.text: The token works for one tool and one customer, and expires in 15 minutes. A leaked token is worth very little.

steps.title: Ask the policy engine at call time
steps.text: Open Policy Agent returns allow, ask_human or deny from the actual arguments. If it returns nothing, the answer is deny.

steps.title: Put a person in front of high-impact actions
steps.text: The INR 18,000 refund goes to the supervisor with a plain summary. The agent waits for the decision.

steps.title: Log every decision
steps.text: Tool, arguments, decision and approver go to an append-only audit log for review and alerting.

steps.title: Cap budgets and keep a kill switch
steps.text: A task that exceeds its call or spend budget is stopped at once, however convincing its reasoning.

pros: Limits damage even when every text filter fails
Deny by default refuses new tools and new attacks automatically
Policies as code are versioned, reviewed and tested
The audit trail answers who did what, when and why
cons: Setup effort: tool inventory, policies and identity plumbing
Approval prompts add delay and can cause approval fatigue
Policies drift from reality unless maintained
avoidWhen: The agent has no tools that read private data or change anything
A throwaway local prototype with no real credentials (add it before any production use)

tools.what: Allow, deny and ask decisions from Rego policies over HTTP

tools.name: MCP authorization
tools.what: OAuth 2.1 access tokens for MCP tool servers

tools.name: OpenTelemetry
tools.what: Vendor-neutral audit traces of every tool call

playgroundGuide.scenario: A support agent can read orders, email customers and issue refunds. It read an email with hidden instructions, so four of the eight tool calls it now attempts were planted by an attacker. Every call passes a policy gate you configure. A supervisor approves genuine requests and rejects planted ones when asked.
controls: Choose what happens to tools the policy doesn’t mention: allow or deny by default.
Restrict email to the ticket’s customer, and choose a shared admin key or a task-scoped token.
Set the refund amount above which a supervisor must approve.

outputs.name: Harmful actions executed
outputs.meaning: Planted calls that actually ran ÷ the 4 planted calls.

outputs.name: Legitimate work completed
outputs.meaning: Genuine calls that ran, automatically or after approval ÷ 4.

outputs.name: Approval prompts
outputs.meaning: How many times the supervisor is interrupted for this one task.

outputs.name: Audit log
outputs.meaning: One line per decision, as it would be stored.

presets.name: Permissive agent
presets.expect: Allow by default, any email recipient, a shared admin key and no approvals up to INR 50,000. Expect all 4 planted calls to run and 0 approval prompts.

presets.name: Zero trust
presets.expect: Deny by default, scoped email, a task-scoped token and approval above INR 10,000. Expect no harmful action, all 4 genuine calls done and 2 approval prompts.

presets.name: Approve every refund
presets.expect: Zero trust with approval for every refund. Expect no harmful action and all genuine work done, but 3 approval prompts, including one for an INR 4,500 refund.

missions.text: Make sure no planted call causes a real side effect.
missions.hint: Deny by default, scope email and tokens, and keep the approval limit below INR 45,000.

missions.text: Stop every harmful action while asking the supervisor only once.
missions.hint: Set the approval limit between INR 20,000 and INR 40,000, so only the unusual refund needs a person.

missions.text: Keep every other control strict, but let exactly one harmful action through by weakening the credential.
missions.hint: Switch to the shared admin key: the cross-customer read succeeds.

tools.best: A general-purpose policy engine: tool-call decisions written in Rego, versioned, unit-tested and queried over HTTP.
tools.ex: POST each tool call to /v1/data/agent/tools/decision and get allow, ask_human or deny back.
pros: Mature, widely deployed and well documented
cons: One more service to run and monitor

tools.best: An authorization language designed to be fast and formally analysable, also behind Amazon Verified Permissions.
tools.ex: permit(principal == Agent::"support", action == Action::"refund", resource) when { context.amount <= 10000 };
pros: Readable policies that can be analysed automatically
cons: Best fit when you model principals and resources carefully

tools.best: OAuth 2.1 access tokens between MCP clients and tool servers, bound to a specific server.
tools.ex: An MCP tool server that accepts only tokens issued for it, with scopes limited to one customer’s orders.
pros: A standard way to scope agent access to tools
Short-lived tokens are recommended in the spec
cons: Fine-grained per-call policy is still your job

tools.best: Isolated cloud sandboxes for code the agent writes and runs.
tools.ex: Run the agent’s data-analysis code in a sandbox with no access to production credentials.
cons: Code and data run outside your own machines

tools.best: MicroVMs that give each agent task strong, VM-level isolation with fast start-up.
tools.ex: Self-host one microVM per coding task, destroyed when the task ends.

tools.best: Emitting every tool call, argument and decision as a trace span to any backend, for audit and alerting.
tools.ex: Alert when one task triggers more than three denied calls in a minute.
cons: Not a policy engine by itself
You design the attributes and retention

goals: Explain least privilege, deny by default and fail closed for tool calls
Choose which actions need human approval without causing approval fatigue
Describe what an audit log for agent actions must record

practice.scenario: An operations agent can read orders, email customers and issue refunds. Every call passes through a policy engine: reads always run, emails may only go to the customer on the ticket, refunds above INR 10,000 wait for a supervisor, and anything else is denied. Every decision is logged for audit.

industries.use: Maker-checker approval for any money movement an agent starts
Agents plan infrastructure changes; a person approves the apply
Least privilege: agents see only records for the current case

practice.analogy: A hotel key card. It opens your room and the gym, only during your stay, and the front desk logs every swipe.

library.name: Open Policy Agent
library.what: The CNCF-graduated policy engine. Rules live in Rego files, are versioned and tested like code, and are queried over HTTP.

samples.code:
import requests, logging

def authorize(tool: str, args: dict, ticket: dict) -> str:
    r = requests.post("http://localhost:8181/v1/data/agent/tools/decision",
                      json={"input": {"tool": tool, "args": args, "ticket": ticket}},
                      timeout=2)
    decision = r.json().get("result", "deny")     # fail closed
    logging.info("policy tool=%s decision=%s args=%s", tool, decision, args)
    return decision                               # "allow" | "ask_human" | "deny"

numericDrill.question: Policy: reads allowed; email only to the ticket's customer; refunds ≤ 10,000 allowed, > 10,000 need a person; everything else denied. Decide: (a) refund 12,500 (b) email a different address (c) delete_user (d) read_orders.
numericDrill.answer: (a) ask a human (b) deny (c) deny, since it isn't listed (d) allow.

interview.question: What does zero trust mean for an AI agent?
interview.answer: Treat every tool call as untrusted whatever the model says: authenticate it, check it against policy when it runs, grant only minimal, short-lived permissions, log it, and require human approval for high-impact actions.

interview.question: How do you avoid approval fatigue?
interview.answer: Gate only high-impact or irreversible actions, show a clear summary of what will happen and why, batch related approvals, and review approval statistics to relax low-risk rules over time.

mistakes.mistake: One long-lived admin key for the agent

mistakes.fix: Deny by default and allow explicitly

quiz.question: Policy: refunds up to and including INR 10,000 are allowed; above that, a supervisor must approve. The agent requests a refund of exactly INR 10,000. What is the decision?
options: allow
ask_human
deny
It depends on the model’s confidence
quiz.explanation: The rule is amount ≤ 10,000, so the boundary value is allowed. Only amounts above it wait for a person.

quiz.question: Policy: reads allowed; send_email only to the ticket’s customer; everything else denied by default. Which calls are denied? Select all that apply.
options: send_email to an address that is not on the ticket
delete_user, which the policy does not list
read_orders for the ticket’s customer
export_customers, which the policy does not list
quiz.explanation: The email breaks its scope, and unlisted tools fall to the default deny. The read is allowed.

quiz.question: An agent summarises the current case. Which credential follows least privilege?
options: Hospital-wide read access to all records
Read-write access to all records, for convenience
Read-only access to this patient’s records, expiring in 15 minutes
A permanent key rotated once a year
quiz.explanation: Scoped to the task, limited to the data needed and short-lived, so a leaked token is worth very little.

quiz.question: The policy engine times out during an outage. What should the gate return for the pending tool call?
options: allow, so customers are not affected
deny: the gate fails closed
Whatever the agent last received
Ask the model to decide
quiz.explanation: An outage is exactly when an attacker would strike. A guardrail must fail closed.

quiz.question: An agent makes 2,000 refund calls a day. With approval required above INR 1,000, 60% of calls need approval. Raising the limit to INR 10,000 means 4% need approval. How many fewer approval prompts is that per day?
An injected research note convinces an agent to call place_order for 10,000 shares. Every text filter missed it. What limits the damage?
options: A stronger system prompt that forbids trading on documents
A policy gate with order limits, scoped credentials and approval
A post-LLM toxicity check on the agent’s order summary
A lower model temperature so the agent acts more predictably
quiz.explanation: Runtime governance acts on the action itself, whatever the model was tricked into saying.

quiz.question: An agent proposes Terraform changes to production. Which setup follows zero trust?
options: The agent plans and applies changes with an admin credential
The agent plans read-only; a person approves the apply step
The agent applies changes after approving its own plan
Every change is applied and logged, but none is gated
quiz.explanation: Irreversible actions wait for a person, and each step gets only the permissions it needs.

quiz.question: A research agent’s output drives a payments agent’s tool calls. Which controls apply? Select all that apply.
options: Treat the research agent’s output as untrusted input
Check each payment call against policy at call time
Give the payments agent its own scoped credentials
Skip checks because both agents are yours
quiz.explanation: One agent’s output can carry an injection into another’s actions, so every call is verified on its own.

quiz.question: A data-analysis agent writes and runs Python on customer-uploaded CSV files. Which control matters most for the execution?
options: Run it on the application server, where the data already sits
Run it in an isolated sandbox with no secrets and limited network
Run it only when the model judges the code to be safe
Run it under the production service account for full access
quiz.explanation: Sandboxing contains whatever the generated code does, including code shaped by a malicious file.

quiz.question: Which fields belong in the audit record of each tool call? Select all that apply.
options: Tool name and arguments
Decision and policy version
Approver identity and timestamp
The agent’s full access token
quiz.explanation: The log must answer who did what, when and why. Storing live tokens would turn the log into a credential leak.

quiz.question: A task’s budget is 40 tool calls or INR 500 of model spend, whichever comes first. A looping task has made 38 calls costing INR 520. What should happen?
options: Continue until it reaches 40 calls
Stop it now: the spend cap is exceeded
Ask the agent whether it is nearly done
Double the budget automatically
quiz.explanation: Either cap stops the task. A budget is enforced in code, however convincing the agent’s reasoning.

quiz.question: Three agents share one admin API key. Which problems does this cause? Select all that apply.
options: Compromising any one agent exposes every permission
The audit log cannot tell which agent made a call
Each agent has more access than its task needs
Tool calls become slower
quiz.explanation: A shared broad key defeats least privilege and attribution. Latency is unaffected.

quiz.question: A developer adds a bulk_export tool but forgets to update the policy. Under deny by default, what happens when the agent calls it?
options: It runs, because new tools are trusted until reviewed
It is denied until someone explicitly allows it
It runs, but every call is written to the audit log
The model decides whether the call looks legitimate
quiz.explanation: Deny by default refuses new tools automatically, which is safer than hoping someone remembers to block them.

quiz.question: A team wants an open-source authorization policy language that is fast and designed for automated analysis of what policies permit. Which fits?
options: Cedar
Microsoft Presidio
Llama Guard
Pydantic
quiz.explanation: Cedar is AWS’s open-source policy language, built for speed and analysability. The others detect PII, classify harm or validate data.

quiz.question: An agent connects to a remote MCP tool server. What does the MCP authorization specification use?
options: OAuth 2.1 access tokens with scopes
A shared password pasted into the system prompt
No authorization when the server is internal
One admin key in an environment variable for all servers
quiz.explanation: MCP’s authorization spec builds on OAuth 2.1, so each client gets scoped, expiring tokens.

quiz.question: An injected email makes a support agent send a merchant’s settlement statement to an outside address. Which policy rule would have stopped it?
options: send_email may go only to the email address on the ticket
The toxicity score of every email must be below 0.5
Emails with attachments must stay under 2 MB each
The agent must restate the ticket number in each email
quiz.explanation: Scoping arguments at call time turns a successful injection into a denied call.

quiz.question: Injection succeeds on 0.5% of 20,000 tasks a day. Refunds up to INR 10,000 run without approval, and each injected request asks for INR 9,999. What is the maximum daily loss?
options: INR 0: the gate stops it
quiz.explanation: 20,000 × 0.5% = 100 attempts × INR 9,999 = INR 9,99,900. An amount limit alone is not enough; add per-customer caps and refund only to the original payment method.

quiz.question: A policy edit accidentally allows refunds above INR 1,00,000 without approval. How should this be prevented?
options: Review every policy by hand once a year
Version policies and run opa test in CI before deploying
Let the agent report any policy that seems wrong
Allow only administrators to talk to the agent
quiz.explanation: Policies are code. Tests for boundary cases catch a wrong comparison before it reaches production.

quiz.question: Which agent actions should wait for human approval? Select all that apply.
options: A NEFT transfer above the approval limit
Closing a customer’s account
Reading the customer’s last five transactions
Waiving a penalty above INR 5,000
quiz.explanation: Gate high-impact or irreversible actions. Routine reads should run without prompts to avoid approval fatigue.

quiz.question: The audit log shows an agent sent 300 emails in two minutes; its normal rate is about 5. What should the runtime controls do?
options: Nothing until the daily report is reviewed
Stop it via the rate cap or kill switch and alert security
Ask the agent to explain why it sent so many
Raise the email quota so the task can finish
quiz.explanation: Budgets and a kill switch stop runaway or hijacked agents at once, and the anomaly alert starts the investigation.
